The communication mixes positive signals (robust job gains, low unemployment) with a strong emphasis on elevated inflation and exogenous supply shocks (Ukraine war, China lockdowns). In a New Keynesian framework with Calvo price-setting and an expectations-augmented Phillips curve (Woodford; Christiano–Eichenbaum–Evans), the 75 bp hike, guidance of “ongoing increases,” and balance-sheet reduction aim to re-anchor inflation expectations, reducing long-run welfare losses from inflation (Walsh; Svensson’s inflation-forecast targeting). However, supply shocks historically worsen the inflation–output trade-off (Blinder and Rudd, 2008), and tighter policy can transmit through the credit channel/financial accelerator to weigh on real activity (Bernanke–Gertler). The operating details—higher IORB and ON RRP rates, QT caps—underscore a clearly hawkish stance consistent with Goodfriend/Meulendyke’s descriptions of interest-rate operating procedures. Net tone is slightly negative due to inflation risks and tightening, tempered by credibility-restoring actions (Volcker-era precedent) and strong labor data.
